options: It runs main() in a separate operating system process
It schedules main() to run every second indefinitely
It converts main() into a regular, non-async function
It creates an event loop, runs the given coroutine to completion, and then closes the loop
questions.explain: asyncio.run() is the standard entry point for an async program: it sets up the event loop, drives the given coroutine to completion, and tears the loop down afterward. It's meant to be called once, at the top level.

questions.q: In plain terms, what does the event loop do?
options: It runs every coroutine in a separate CPU core simultaneously
It's a single-threaded scheduler that sets aside a coroutine when it awaits something slow, runs other ready coroutines, and resumes the first one once its wait is over
It repeatedly restarts the whole program until it succeeds
It compiles Python code into machine code for faster execution
questions.explain: The event loop is single-threaded. Its job is to overlap waiting time: when a coroutine awaits something slow, the loop switches to another coroutine that's ready to make progress, rather than blocking the whole program.

questions.q: Why does the two-`await`-in-a-row example (`await asyncio.sleep(1)` twice) still take about 2 seconds, not 1?
options: Each await fully waits for its own coroutine to finish before the next line runs — await alone doesn't create concurrency
asyncio.sleep() is broken and always takes twice as long
Python requires a minimum 2-second delay for any async function
The event loop only allows one asyncio.sleep() call per program
questions.explain: await just means "run this and pause here until it's done." Chaining two awaits back to back is still sequential — concurrency requires starting both operations before awaiting either, which is what create_task() is for.

questions.q: What does `asyncio.create_task()` do that a plain `await` does not?
options: It deletes the coroutine without running it
It pauses the entire program until the task is manually resumed
It schedules the coroutine to start running immediately in the background, returning a Task you can await later — enabling true concurrency
It only works with synchronous functions, not coroutines
questions.explain: create_task() kicks a coroutine off running right away, without blocking. Multiple create_task() calls can all be in flight before you await any of them, which is what lets their waits overlap.

questions.q: In the lesson's final example, why does `await t1` followed by `await t2` take roughly 1 second total instead of 2, when each task sleeps for 1 second?
options: Because await automatically halves all wait times
Because asyncio.sleep() ignores its argument the second time it's called
Because t2 doesn't actually run at all
Because both tasks were already started concurrently with create_task() before either was awaited, so their 1-second waits overlap
questions.explain: Both t1 and t2 were already running in the background by the time the awaits happen (thanks to create_task()), so their waits overlap — the two awaits are just collecting results from work that's already mostly or fully done.
